Desmond D'Sa and Kevin Kimwelle

By: Sophia Phirippides | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Winner of the internationally prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014, Desmond D'Sa continues his decades long fight for environmental justice, especially in his South Durban hometown.

Unique Selling Point:
During Apartheid, Desmond and his family were uprooted from their home and dumped in an industry intensive area of South Durban. There he witnessed the environmental damage that can be caused by mishandled waste and embarked on a lifetime of campaigning for the now constitutionally protected right to a safe and clean environment. In 1996, he co-founded the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) which is still highly active today.

Through his tireless work Desmond D'Sa came to the attention of the international environmental movement and won the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014 primarily for his unstinting opposition to the hazardous waste fallout from the Bulbul Drive landfill site and his monitoring and actions in "cancer valley", the South Durban basin notorious for its high incidences of leukaemia, asthma and bronchitis, due to toxic waste from the conglomerate of large scale industrial plants in the area. Desmond will take us on a tour of this area.

Details of KEVIN KIMWELLE at end of Further information:

Summary:
To keep up with what Desmond D’Sa is campaigning on would be a full time job in itself. Only this week he is in the news with The South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) with their appeal against a decision by the Department of Mineral Resources to grant Sasol and Italian multinational oil and gas company ENI environmental authorisation to explore for oil and gas along the North and South coasts of KwaZulu-Natal.

Desmond’s bread and butter though is tacking the fallout from local industry waste that is acutely affecting the health of people in the local communities of Durban South. Under President Mandela, an extensive system of monitoring and reporting was set up to keep tags on the situation, but it collapsed and now D’Sa and his organizations have actioned their own systems including the detection of the levels of Benzene and recording and bringing to attention the levels of cancers like leukaemia in the area.

Desmond D’Sa is at the forefront of the struggle to ensure a clean environment, for the people living and working in the midst of heavy industry, where environmental regulation is severely absent.

Further information:
We will film Desmond in South Durban at the various interfaces of his campaign work, including demonstrations of monitoring and detection activities. We will interview him for context, his campaign successes and disappointments, the current state of environmental challenges and film local people to hear harrowing personal stories of the dismal effects of living in the shadow of minimally regulated industry.

Relevant issues include:

How Desmond D’Sa rallied south Durban’s diverse and disenfranchised communities and successfully shut down a toxic waste dump.

The death threats and attempts on his life to those who oppose his campaigns.

The current conditions in “cancer valley”- almost 70 percent of Durban’s industry is in south Durban, home to more than 300 industrial-scale facilities such as oil and gas refineries, paper mills, and agrochemical plants. It is also home to 300,000 residents, mostly low-income and working-class people who were forcibly relocated here by the apartheid regime to create a cheap labour pool for the emerging industrial economy and who suffer unbearably from poor health and safety.

The successful fight against the expansion of Durban’s port, that was to displace thousands of people without compensation and exacerbate problems such as waste management, pollution, and traffic.

Desmond’s current battle against unfettered exploration for oil and gas all along the KZN coastline.

We will need to provide a right of reply to the particular companies implicated by Desmond’s campaigns.

---

KEVIN KIMWELLE

One Liner:

Can recycled waste be turned into award winning architecture and create functional living and work spaces? Kevin Kimwelle is doing it. Imagine a school made partly from empty wine bottles?


Unique Selling Point:

Kenya-born architect and social entrepreneur, Kevin Kimwelle came to study architecture at the Walter Sisulu University in 2006 and is now busy with his doctorate. Kevin wanted to work with communities and transform townships, PE being a motor city inspired him to look at waste as a means of building and creating new spaces and objects. He collects recycled and discarded materials from informal recyclers and local businesses, and uses it to construct his buildings, which so far include a school, recycling depots, rainwater tanks and even solar panels.

Kevin also supplements the local collectors of recyclable waste, by designing custom designed bikes with trailers and store areas for recyclable waste dealers to keep their produce secure before they trade them.


Summary:

In 2018 with Kimwelle at the head as lead architect, the Joe Slovo Community Project (Joe Slovo township, north Port Elizabeth) won the coveted 2018 SAPOA (South African Property Association) Awards for the most transformative project in South Africa competing against the Seitz Mocaa Museum – V&A Waterfront- Cape Town, and the Waterfall City – Johannesburg, the later two having budgets in the billions of rands these accolades make the larger community aware of non-mainstream alternative development space, encourage social innovation grounding the green agenda.

However, functionality isn’t the end of the story. A healthy environment in which to live also involves the aesthetics of design. Kimwelle had this very much in mind and in 2017 the Silindokuhle Creche, an innovative building central to the Joe Slovo Community Project, was nominated at Cape Town’s Design Indaba as one of 2017’s most beautiful objects in South Africa. With the help of the community, Kimwelle designed and built a structure made entirely of recycled materials – including 2,500 wine bottles. The glass bottle walls create an illuminated, rather magical atmosphere inside the building. We visit this remarkable man in PE and meet some of the people who’s lives he has touched and transformed.


Further Details:

In time for Christmas, Kimwelle is building a house for Selina, a deaf resident of Joe Slovo township. We will film the project as it is now with Kevin and Selina. This along with the other buildings, vehicles and structures he has manufactured in the area.
Although originally from Kenya, Kimwelle has had no experience of xenophobia, and as part of the north Port Elizabeth community strives to trigger change, economically viable and environmentally friendly. A self made operation giving hope and worth to the wider community, a beacon of possibilities for transformational development on the ground.

Visually, we aim to chart an inspirational tour of architectural and design in PE, built from home grown and collected recycled materials and guided by Kevin Kimwelle who, encouraged by recognition in South Africa and over-seas continues to strive for social upliftment in South Africa’s townships.

Press Release:


Winner of the internationally prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014, Desmond D'Sa continues his decades long fight for environmental justice, especially in his South Durban hometown.

Can recycled waste be turned into award winning architecture and create functional living and work spaces? Kevin Kimwelle is doing it. Imagine a school made partly from empty wine bottles?

Script:


Desmond D'Sa Eco Warrior

VO: In the heart of Durban South lives a shining light amidst the dirty secret of industrial pollution , an extra ordinary South African, eco warrior and environmental champion Desmond D'Sa, who has made it his life long mission to fight for a safer and cleaner environment.


Desmond: Well the major toxic offenders are the chemical and petrochemical industry. Over 300 of the most toxic class 1 carcinogenic chemicals are brought into South Durban daily.

LINK: This is cancer Alley in the south of Durban. It's where thousands of people live and work amidst the toxic fallout of industry.

VO: Locals call it cancer alley because excessive emissions of Benzene, a known carcinogen are prominent in the air.
Anecdotally communities in the area allege that there are many cases of respiratory diseases and leukemia.

Desmond: So at the moment we are collecting information from all the people that have died, including those with cancer and asthma, so that we can release it.

Derek: Desmond you were around 15 when the family was uprooted and you were forced to live amidst the pollution?

Desmond: It was just during the Group Areas Act and my dad worked in the motor industry and then my brothers and sister worked in the clothing industry. Then we started to smell all the chemicals in the air, my father got yellow jaundice, because of that he died And my mother was sick and a year later she went in 1981.

Derek: You lost family members possibly because of the pollution.

Desmond: it's only when I started to work in the chemical industry. And then I realized what we were what we were breathing in. Because I was a risk assessor, made me realize that you know we haven't been told the truth.

VO: After witnessing the personal and environmental damage that can be caused by mishandled waste, in 1996, D'Sa co-founded the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) which still fights for the now constitutionally protected right to a safe and clean environment.

Desmond: When I saw that people were prepared to stand up for a common purpose no matter what our diversities It's what taught me that everything is possible.

VO: Along with one of his next generation eco warriors Bongani Mthembu, we set off to the scene of one of D'Sa's greatest successes, the closure of the Bulbul Drive landfill in 2011.

Desmond: That site has been where the chemicals have been dumped over the years. That's one of the one of the three toxic landfill sites that we have shut down

VO: But even now, here at the decommissioned Bulbul landfill, the putrid smell of chemicals still lingers.

Derek: Bongani, fancy piece of equipment this. What does it do?

Bongani: Basically this is a monitor. It's called The Tiger, so it can analyze up to 400 different chemicals.

Derek: Can we test for something?

Bongani: We can test for VOCs, it's a host of different pollutants it's organic compounds. Basically whenever it picks up any pollutants it will give you a reading.

VO: The reading on the detector was 0.3 parts per million for pollutants in the air, a general indicator of air quality rather than specific chemicals

Derek:
Is that good or bad?

Bongani: It's bad because its pollution, its chemicals that people are exposed to.

Desmond: There is still a big smell. It will be there for the next 30, 40 years

VO: D'Sa and his team are tireless in their efforts and continuously monitor air pollution especially around the Durban Bluff area.

Derek: Are you getting a reading already?

Bongani: Yeah just setting it

Derek: What's that for, benzene? You can smell it hey.
Desmond: You can smell it, It's strong...
Derek: I'm seeing school kids, its center of the community all around. I wouldn't like to live amidst this.

VO: Bongani also monitors the area with another air sniffer the bucket, and over a period of time some readings have exceeded the South African limit by far.

Desmond: There's a block of flats right here. There's 9 people in one block, all got cancer.

Derek: So what have you done about it?

Desmond: We've shared the information with the city, we've campaigned vigorously on that.

VO: And D'Sa's fight for a cleaner world was vindicated with an international accolade.

Sound Up:
Outsourced Footage\Desmond\Desmond D'Sa, 2014 Goldman Environmental Prize, South Africa.mp4

For outstanding environmental achievement in Africa, the 2014 Goldman Environmental Prize is awarded to Desmond D’Sa, Durban, South Africa.

LINK: One of Desmond's biggest environmental battles of recent years has been against oil exploration off the KZN coastline. The possibility of massive oil rigs about 60 kilometres out to sea.

Desmond: Operation Phakisa never brought the facts out the entire coastline was sold in blocks.

VO: Operation Phakisa is a government initiative, which has enabled the promotion of a number of commercial activities on South Africa's oceans, including gas and oil extraction and exploratory drilling in the Durban and Zululand basins.

Desmond: We've got millions of people coming in December to this ocean enjoying the beach. If there is oil spill we are going to swim. Where the oil companies have been, whether its Mozambique, whether it's in Nigeria. People have never benefited. There's been no jobs. In fact the opposite has happened.

LINK: Fighting for the environment may seem glamorous and it's certainly for a worthy cause. But there are definite risks

Desmond: I've been I've been threatened but I've crossed that river now and I've come to understand we are standing up against big big money who really put interest of money first and don't really care about the planet and the environment and people.

Derek: Do all the protests and rallies really help?

Desmond: It helps tremendously, because as we are united as South Africans we can win against everything.

Derek: What's the environmental legacy that you want to leave behind.

Desmond: Well for me is that another World Is Possible, a world that is clean, that's healthy, We only have one planet. I want to see our kids enjoy that. Then I can say you know yeah that's my future.
Derek: The fight has been worth it.
Desmond: The fight has been worth it.

---

Kevin Kimwelle, activist architect

VO: Architecture and design is hallowed ground for the elite, but Kenyan born activist-architect Kevin Kimwelle, wants to make it accessible for everyone and he is pioneering the way in the townships of his adopted city, Port Elizabeth.

Kevin: In Port Elizabeth which is a motor industry, there's a lot of recycled material that we can reuse. The architecture that I'm pursuing looks at certain things. One is the green agenda which is the whole idea of recycling, reuse, up cycling, repurposing materials right from within the community or within the city. A lot of the shacks in the townships are actually built out of pallets, scrap metal. So the idea was then introduce design and increase the value of the material.

VO: Kimwelle, whose doctoral research is centered at Nelson Mandela University, put his flair for innovation into action when building the Silindokuhle Creche in Joe Slovo Township. It was nominated at Cape Town's Design Indaba as one of 2017's most beautiful objects in South Africa.

Kevin: The whole wall is 2500 wine bottles of different colour. We invited restaurants and we had to go in and collect a specific bottle, clean it and have it ready to go into this wall.

VO: The bottles created a kaleidoscope of light and soon the building became an activity hub in the township. But over a period of time, it fell prey to political infighting and was partially damaged. Kimwelle is here to see what repairs are needed.

Kevin: At that stage there was no infrastructure. There was no RDP houses around it or anything. So it played a very pivotal role in the transition between informal settlements into formal settlements.
VO: Socio economic impact is a key driver for Kimwelle, enabling eco friendly workspaces and skills transferral, like this spaza shop right next to the creche. In order to implement these challenging ideas he needed to get funders on board.

Kevin: It was very difficult to convince people that we could build out of recycled material, because it is perceived by our community or by society to be inferior.


VO: One way of showcasing the potential was to live it. He refurbished his home using pallets and other reusables. // And his work did get noticed. Ncodisa Mzuzu heads up environmental management for Isuzu and has worked closely with Kimwelle on some of his projects.

Ncodisa: Waste is quite a serious issue in Port Elizabeth, Instead of taking it down the waste hierarchy, we partnered with Kevin to rather upcycle and use the material for beneficial use of the beneficiaries that we've chosen.

VO: Some community members do know the value of waste, like 56 year old waste collector Kusta Moko, who recently had an accident.

Kusta: A car was coming from somewhere and it pushed my trolley away from the road, when I saw the trolley was broken into pieces.

Kevin: I've known him for 2 or 3 years and I've been watching his journey, and I thought, well I'm sure we could do something to improve it.

VO: He had the idea of building 2 carts made from at least 80% recyclables and using discarded motor industry parts. Kusta is at Kimwelle's workshop for a test drive, eager to get them on the road.

Kusta: It makes it very easy for me, because it’s got lights, so each and every car coming from the back, will see there is someone in the road.

VO: A visionary, Kimwelle wants to build one of the most advanced structures from 2 litre bottles or - eco bricks, for Principal Blommie Nontshinga’s creche.

Blommie: Eco Brick is helping us clean up our area because it’s full of plastic and the community came one time and collected all the plastic around our area, and put the plastic in this bottle and then this is how they're going to build our creche, by using these bottles.

Kevin: That eco brick will then go into a building and the function of the eco brick is thermal mass, which means it retains heat.

Blommie: There's lots of shacks so I'm sure if they see how they use the eco brick to build our creche, that’s what they're also going to do and we're going to have more clean area than it is now.

VO: Working closely with the communities, Kimwelle gets to hear about people in need, and the plight of 80 year old Selina Ncanywa was brought to his attention.

Kevin: Selena to me represents a lot of the older black South Africans. She lives in a one room house that she's kind of extended in the front in the back. Her daughter had died at childbirth to a grandchild who she's raising up. She can hardly hear much and her vision is not so great either.

VO: Kimwelle had some wonderful news for Selina, he and some sponsors are are building her a new home for Christmas.

Kevin: The idea is a house made out of recycled material, but a shelter that is weatherproof that kind of gives her some pride.

VO: When Kimwelle showed her the designs, Selina was visibly moved.


Selina: I can be glad, you can come here.

Translator: She says she will be very glad.

Translator: You will get everything for Christmas.

Selina: He who we pray to, understands everything.

Translator: The lord that she prays to, understands everything. So it's really close to her heart.
Selina: Because we worship him, you know.

Ncodisa: I think Kevin is an inventor, but most importantly I think the compassion and the nature in which the projects are done, it's not a tick in the box but it's about changing lifestyles of people.

Kevin: My vision is to be able to scale this to the entire continent of Africa and also to the globe, to the whole world. I mean we are all global citizens.

mihle@combinedartists.co.za 09 December 2019 Press Release: Winner of the internationally prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014, Desmond D'Sa continues his decades long fight for environmental justice, especially in his South Durban hometown. Can recycled waste be turned into award winning architecture and create functional living and work spaces? Kevin Kimwelle is doing it. Imagine a school made partly from empty wine bottles? Script: Desmond D'Sa Eco Warrior VO: In the heart of Durban South lives a shining light amidst the dirty secret of industrial pollution , an extra ordinary South African, eco warrior and environmental champion Desmond D'Sa, who has made it his life long mission to fight for a safer and cleaner environment. Desmond: Well the major toxic offenders are the chemical and petrochemical industry. Over 300 of the most toxic class 1 carcinogenic chemicals are brought into South Durban daily. LINK: This is cancer Alley in the south of Durban. It's where thousands of people live and work amidst the toxic fallout of industry. VO: Locals call it cancer alley because excessive emissions of Benzene, a known carcinogen are prominent in the air. Anecdotally communities in the area allege that there are many cases of respiratory diseases and leukemia. Desmond: So at the moment we are collecting information from all the people that have died, including those with cancer and asthma, so that we can release it. Derek: Desmond you were around 15 when the family was uprooted and you were forced to live amidst the pollution? Desmond: It was just during the Group Areas Act and my dad worked in the motor industry and then my brothers and sister worked in the clothing industry. Then we started to smell all the chemicals in the air, my father got yellow jaundice, because of that he died And my mother was sick and a year later she went in 1981. Derek: You lost family members possibly because of the pollution. Desmond: it's only when I started to work in the chemical industry. And then I realized what we were what we were breathing in. Because I was a risk assessor, made me realize that you know we haven't been told the truth. VO: After witnessing the personal and environmental damage that can be caused by mishandled waste, in 1996, D'Sa co-founded the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) which still fights for the now constitutionally protected right to a safe and clean environment. Desmond: When I saw that people were prepared to stand up for a common purpose no matter what our diversities It's what taught me that everything is possible. VO: Along with one of his next generation eco warriors Bongani Mthembu, we set off to the scene of one of D'Sa's greatest successes, the closure of the Bulbul Drive landfill in 2011. Desmond: That site has been where the chemicals have been dumped over the years. That's one of the one of the three toxic landfill sites that we have shut down VO: But even now, here at the decommissioned Bulbul landfill, the putrid smell of chemicals still lingers. Derek: Bongani, fancy piece of equipment this. What does it do? Bongani: Basically this is a monitor. It's called The Tiger, so it can analyze up to 400 different chemicals. Derek: Can we test for something? Bongani: We can test for VOCs, it's a host of different pollutants it's organic compounds. Basically whenever it picks up any pollutants it will give you a reading. VO: The reading on the detector was 0.3 parts per million for pollutants in the air, a general indicator of air quality rather than specific chemicals Derek: Is that good or bad? Bongani: It's bad because its pollution, its chemicals that people are exposed to. Desmond: There is still a big smell. It will be there for the next 30, 40 years VO: D'Sa and his team are tireless in their efforts and continuously monitor air pollution especially around the Durban Bluff area. Derek: Are you getting a reading already? Bongani: Yeah just setting it Derek: What's that for, benzene? You can smell it hey. Desmond: You can smell it, It's strong... Derek: I'm seeing school kids, its center of the community all around. I wouldn't like to live amidst this. VO: Bongani also monitors the area with another air sniffer the bucket, and over a period of time some readings have exceeded the South African limit by far. Desmond: There's a block of flats right here. There's 9 people in one block, all got cancer. Derek: So what have you done about it? Desmond: We've shared the information with the city, we've campaigned vigorously on that. VO: And D'Sa's fight for a cleaner world was vindicated with an international accolade. Sound Up: Outsourced Footage\Desmond\Desmond D'Sa, 2014 Goldman Environmental Prize, South Africa.mp4 For outstanding environmental achievement in Africa, the 2014 Goldman Environmental Prize is awarded to Desmond D’Sa, Durban, South Africa. LINK: One of Desmond's biggest environmental battles of recent years has been against oil exploration off the KZN coastline. The possibility of massive oil rigs about 60 kilometres out to sea. Desmond: Operation Phakisa never brought the facts out the entire coastline was sold in blocks. VO: Operation Phakisa is a government initiative, which has enabled the promotion of a number of commercial activities on South Africa's oceans, including gas and oil extraction and exploratory drilling in the Durban and Zululand basins. Desmond: We've got millions of people coming in December to this ocean enjoying the beach. If there is oil spill we are going to swim. Where the oil companies have been, whether its Mozambique, whether it's in Nigeria. People have never benefited. There's been no jobs. In fact the opposite has happened. LINK: Fighting for the environment may seem glamorous and it's certainly for a worthy cause. But there are definite risks Desmond: I've been I've been threatened but I've crossed that river now and I've come to understand we are standing up against big big money who really put interest of money first and don't really care about the planet and the environment and people. Derek: Do all the protests and rallies really help? Desmond: It helps tremendously, because as we are united as South Africans we can win against everything. Derek: What's the environmental legacy that you want to leave behind. Desmond: Well for me is that another World Is Possible, a world that is clean, that's healthy, We only have one planet. I want to see our kids enjoy that. Then I can say you know yeah that's my future. Derek: The fight has been worth it. Desmond: The fight has been worth it. --- Kevin Kimwelle, activist architect VO: Architecture and design is hallowed ground for the elite, but Kenyan born activist-architect Kevin Kimwelle, wants to make it accessible for everyone and he is pioneering the way in the townships of his adopted city, Port Elizabeth. Kevin: In Port Elizabeth which is a motor industry, there's a lot of recycled material that we can reuse. The architecture that I'm pursuing looks at certain things. One is the green agenda which is the whole idea of recycling, reuse, up cycling, repurposing materials right from within the community or within the city. A lot of the shacks in the townships are actually built out of pallets, scrap metal. So the idea was then introduce design and increase the value of the material. VO: Kimwelle, whose doctoral research is centered at Nelson Mandela University, put his flair for innovation into action when building the Silindokuhle Creche in Joe Slovo Township. It was nominated at Cape Town's Design Indaba as one of 2017's most beautiful objects in South Africa. Kevin: The whole wall is 2500 wine bottles of different colour. We invited restaurants and we had to go in and collect a specific bottle, clean it and have it ready to go into this wall. VO: The bottles created a kaleidoscope of light and soon the building became an activity hub in the township. But over a period of time, it fell prey to political infighting and was partially damaged. Kimwelle is here to see what repairs are needed. Kevin: At that stage there was no infrastructure. There was no RDP houses around it or anything. So it played a very pivotal role in the transition between informal settlements into formal settlements. VO: Socio economic impact is a key driver for Kimwelle, enabling eco friendly workspaces and skills transferral, like this spaza shop right next to the creche. In order to implement these challenging ideas he needed to get funders on board. Kevin: It was very difficult to convince people that we could build out of recycled material, because it is perceived by our community or by society to be inferior. VO: One way of showcasing the potential was to live it. He refurbished his home using pallets and other reusables. // And his work did get noticed. Ncodisa Mzuzu heads up environmental management for Isuzu and has worked closely with Kimwelle on some of his projects. Ncodisa: Waste is quite a serious issue in Port Elizabeth, Instead of taking it down the waste hierarchy, we partnered with Kevin to rather upcycle and use the material for beneficial use of the beneficiaries that we've chosen. VO: Some community members do know the value of waste, like 56 year old waste collector Kusta Moko, who recently had an accident. Kusta: A car was coming from somewhere and it pushed my trolley away from the road, when I saw the trolley was broken into pieces. Kevin: I've known him for 2 or 3 years and I've been watching his journey, and I thought, well I'm sure we could do something to improve it. VO: He had the idea of building 2 carts made from at least 80% recyclables and using discarded motor industry parts. Kusta is at Kimwelle's workshop for a test drive, eager to get them on the road. Kusta: It makes it very easy for me, because it’s got lights, so each and every car coming from the back, will see there is someone in the road. VO: A visionary, Kimwelle wants to build one of the most advanced structures from 2 litre bottles or - eco bricks, for Principal Blommie Nontshinga’s creche. Blommie: Eco Brick is helping us clean up our area because it’s full of plastic and the community came one time and collected all the plastic around our area, and put the plastic in this bottle and then this is how they're going to build our creche, by using these bottles. Kevin: That eco brick will then go into a building and the function of the eco brick is thermal mass, which means it retains heat. Blommie: There's lots of shacks so I'm sure if they see how they use the eco brick to build our creche, that’s what they're also going to do and we're going to have more clean area than it is now. VO: Working closely with the communities, Kimwelle gets to hear about people in need, and the plight of 80 year old Selina Ncanywa was brought to his attention. Kevin: Selena to me represents a lot of the older black South Africans. She lives in a one room house that she's kind of extended in the front in the back. Her daughter had died at childbirth to a grandchild who she's raising up. She can hardly hear much and her vision is not so great either. VO: Kimwelle had some wonderful news for Selina, he and some sponsors are are building her a new home for Christmas. Kevin: The idea is a house made out of recycled material, but a shelter that is weatherproof that kind of gives her some pride. VO: When Kimwelle showed her the designs, Selina was visibly moved. Selina: I can be glad, you can come here. Translator: She says she will be very glad. Translator: You will get everything for Christmas. Selina: He who we pray to, understands everything. Translator: The lord that she prays to, understands everything. So it's really close to her heart. Selina: Because we worship him, you know. Ncodisa: I think Kevin is an inventor, but most importantly I think the compassion and the nature in which the projects are done, it's not a tick in the box but it's about changing lifestyles of people. Kevin: My vision is to be able to scale this to the entire continent of Africa and also to the globe, to the whole world. I mean we are all global citizens.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): Winner of the internationally prestigious Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014, Desmond D'Sa continues his decades long fight for environmental justice, especially in his South Durban hometown.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: During Apartheid, Desmond and his family were uprooted from their home and dumped in an industry intensive area of South Durban. There he witnessed the environmental damage that can be caused by mishandled waste and embarked on a lifetime of campaigning for the now constitutionally protected right to a safe and clean environment. In 1996, he co-founded the South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) which is still highly active today. Through his tireless work Desmond D'Sa came to the attention of the international environmental movement and won the Goldman Environmental Prize in 2014 primarily for his unstinting opposition to the hazardous waste fallout from the Bulbul Drive landfill site and his monitoring and actions in "cancer valley", the South Durban basin notorious for its high incidences of leukaemia, asthma and bronchitis, due to toxic waste from the conglomerate of large scale industrial plants in the area. Desmond will take us on a tour of this area. Details of KEVIN KIMWELLE at end of Further information:
metadata.Summary: To keep up with what Desmond D’Sa is campaigning on would be a full time job in itself. Only this week he is in the news with The South Durban Community Environmental Alliance (SDCEA) with their appeal against a decision by the Department of Mineral Resources to grant Sasol and Italian multinational oil and gas company ENI environmental authorisation to explore for oil and gas along the North and South coasts of KwaZulu-Natal. Desmond’s bread and butter though is tacking the fallout from local industry waste that is acutely affecting the health of people in the local communities of Durban South. Under President Mandela, an extensive system of monitoring and reporting was set up to keep tags on the situation, but it collapsed and now D’Sa and his organizations have actioned their own systems including the detection of the levels of Benzene and recording and bringing to attention the levels of cancers like leukaemia in the area. Desmond D’Sa is at the forefront of the struggle to ensure a clean environment, for the people living and working in the midst of heavy industry, where environmental regulation is severely absent.
metadata.Further information: We will film Desmond in South Durban at the various interfaces of his campaign work, including demonstrations of monitoring and detection activities. We will interview him for context, his campaign successes and disappointments, the current state of environmental challenges and film local people to hear harrowing personal stories of the dismal effects of living in the shadow of minimally regulated industry. Relevant issues include: How Desmond D’Sa rallied south Durban’s diverse and disenfranchised communities and successfully shut down a toxic waste dump. The death threats and attempts on his life to those who oppose his campaigns. The current conditions in “cancer valley”- almost 70 percent of Durban’s industry is in south Durban, home to more than 300 industrial-scale facilities such as oil and gas refineries, paper mills, and agrochemical plants. It is also home to 300,000 residents, mostly low-income and working-class people who were forcibly relocated here by the apartheid regime to create a cheap labour pool for the emerging industrial economy and who suffer unbearably from poor health and safety. The successful fight against the expansion of Durban’s port, that was to displace thousands of people without compensation and exacerbate problems such as waste management, pollution, and traffic. Desmond’s current battle against unfettered exploration for oil and gas all along the KZN coastline. We will need to provide a right of reply to the particular companies implicated by Desmond’s campaigns. --- KEVIN KIMWELLE One Liner: Can recycled waste be turned into award winning architecture and create functional living and work spaces? Kevin Kimwelle is doing it. Imagine a school made partly from empty wine bottles? Unique Selling Point: Kenya-born architect and social entrepreneur, Kevin Kimwelle came to study architecture at the Walter Sisulu University in 2006 and is now busy with his doctorate. Kevin wanted to work with communities and transform townships, PE being a motor city inspired him to look at waste as a means of building and creating new spaces and objects. He collects recycled and discarded materials from informal recyclers and local businesses, and uses it to construct his buildings, which so far include a school, recycling depots, rainwater tanks and even solar panels. Kevin also supplements the local collectors of recyclable waste, by designing custom designed bikes with trailers and store areas for recyclable waste dealers to keep their produce secure before they trade them. Summary: In 2018 with Kimwelle at the head as lead architect, the Joe Slovo Community Project (Joe Slovo township, north Port Elizabeth) won the coveted 2018 SAPOA (South African Property Association) Awards for the most transformative project in South Africa competing against the Seitz Mocaa Museum – V&A Waterfront- Cape Town, and the Waterfall City – Johannesburg, the later two having budgets in the billions of rands these accolades make the larger community aware of non-mainstream alternative development space, encourage social innovation grounding the green agenda. However, functionality isn’t the end of the story. A healthy environment in which to live also involves the aesthetics of design. Kimwelle had this very much in mind and in 2017 the Silindokuhle Creche, an innovative building central to the Joe Slovo Community Project, was nominated at Cape Town’s Design Indaba as one of 2017’s most beautiful objects in South Africa. With the help of the community, Kimwelle designed and built a structure made entirely of recycled materials – including 2,500 wine bottles. The glass bottle walls create an illuminated, rather magical atmosphere inside the building. We visit this remarkable man in PE and meet some of the people who’s lives he has touched and transformed. Further Details: In time for Christmas, Kimwelle is building a house for Selina, a deaf resident of Joe Slovo township. We will film the project as it is now with Kevin and Selina. This along with the other buildings, vehicles and structures he has manufactured in the area. Although originally from Kenya, Kimwelle has had no experience of xenophobia, and as part of the north Port Elizabeth community strives to trigger change, economically viable and environmentally friendly. A self made operation giving hope and worth to the wider community, a beacon of possibilities for transformational development on the ground. Visually, we aim to chart an inspirational tour of architectural and design in PE, built from home grown and collected recycled materials and guided by Kevin Kimwelle who, encouraged by recognition in South Africa and over-seas continues to strive for social upliftment in South Africa’s townships.
